newsitem.title: UK: Surplus capacity depresses ex-UK/America air rates.
newsitem.headline: Surplus capacity depresses ex-UK/America air rates.

text.p: LONDON, July 3 - Air cargo rates across the Atlantic from the UK are being depressed by excess lower deck capacity generated from additional passenger flights, a Reuters survey showed.

"The injection of extra capacity has put rates under big pressure and there is now excess belly capacity," said Kevin Durnin managing director of Viking Freight Services - a UK cargo general sales agent.
As a result some carriers are prepared to carry freight at on what may be package holiday charters or extra scheduled flights at very low rates, industry sources said.

This situation was underlined by major cargo wholesalers Air Menzies International (AMI) who for July are offering ex-UK flat "incentive" rates for seven U.S. cities to each of which it is offering two rates - above and below 3 cu m. The cities are Atlanta, Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles, New York, Philadelphia and San Francisco.

AMI general manager (commercial) Sharon Wright said Miami was not an important U.S. gateway for AMI so was excluded. Miami is probably suffering the severest rate cutting owing to the weight of holiday traffic to Florida.

AMI's lowest rates were to New York at 35 pence per kg for under 3 cu m and 45 pence for over. The highest under the incentive scheme were to Houston and San Francisco at 60 pence per kilo under and 63 pence over 3 cu m.
Rates to Latin America have also softened with forwarders and shippers having more options as there is less traffic chasing more capacity, Wright said.
For the U.S. this is likely to continue except for the annual pre-Christmas rush, she added.
Air Canada cargo manager for the UK and Ireland Mike Judkins said that whilst it is flying full planes at the weekend it has empty space midweek.

"The excess capacity is likely to keep rates under pressure for another three months before a reduction in passenger flights allows the (cargo) market to recover," he added. Last month Air Canada started an Internet site on which it will post available cargo space.

The battle for cargo across the Atlantic has meant Air Canada has switched some flights in favour of passengers by substituting passenger 747s for Combis. At current rates on direct ex-UK to U.S. flights, Air Canada could not compete flying via Toronto, he added.
Both carriers and forwarders said the strength of sterling was dampening demand for airfreight from the UK and noted that in comparison, business from Europe is better.

Forwarding agents said the importance of currency fluctuations was illustrated by an earlier decision by Intel to source computer components for Japan to a west coast U.S. factory and away from one at Shannon in Ireland. The latter had required a weekly Aeroflot charter flight.

Cargo agents said they believed the decision directly reflected the rise in the Irish punt against the dollar in recent months although a recent slide in the Irish currency against sterling caused most carriers which have sterling expenses to place a surcharge, albeit temporary, on Irish punt cargo rates. These had originally been set on the assumption of parity between the two currencies, Irish forwarders said.

The gloomy picture of excess transatlantic lower deck cargo capacity was lightened by some glamour interest with Lufthansa flying a mix of 25 rather special vintage or racing cars from Atlanta, Chicago and New York to Prestwick in Scotland in 747-400F for a motoring festival at Goodwood in the south of England. Lufthansa flew the cars back to their homes in the U.S. last week.

Another unusual recent cargo was Virgin Atlantic's flying of the collection of 79 dresses owned by Princess Diana to New York for last week's auction expected to raise millions of dollars for AIDS and cancer charities.

Apart from flat rate incentives the main downward pressure came on rates for shipments of at least 500 kg and more especially for those of over one tonne on routes popular with holiday charter flights or where scheduled carriers had introduced additional flights to meet passenger demand.

The lowest rates for smaller packages were only available from forwarders prepared to pass on part of the heavily discounted pallet or containers rates offered by some carriers. Such consolidated consignments obviously had more restricted terms making them a poor guide to average rates.
The other pressure point was in mid-week flights where spare capacity was most noticeable.
Durnin said "big hits" of one tonne or over, especially for dense cargoes, were able to get rates of below 40 pence per kg to Miami.

Carriers flying dedicated freighters with main deck capacity said their rates did not come under the same pressure. Likewise carriers with an established client base who had not made significant changes to their capacity said they were able to fly with high yields without entering the price cutting game.
Most carriers said that shipments of 100 kg were being left out of this latest plunge in the air cargo roller-coaster.
"It's simply not worth our while to chase small shipments at these low rates," said one major carrier.

The impact of this was a further widening of the discount for larger shipments over small packages with the lowest rates for the latter probably available through forwarders filling pallets or containers which they said were still being made available at very low rates by British Airways.
One top carrier said of the rates war that it would fly nothing across the Atlantic for under 60 pence a kg, regardless of what others were prepared to accept.
There was general agreement that logic did not always play a part in determining differentials between routes, Instead it was a simple tussle of supply and demand in an open market place.

Likewise some carriers quoted rates that dipped below 40 pence a kilo to Miami for high density cargo of at least 500 kg. This contrasting with a wide range of available rates of under 50 to over 60 pence per kg for 100 kg loads.

Much of this lower deck cargo arriving in Florida is either being trucked to other destinations like Atlanta or Houston or is being transhipped to Latin America thereby putting pressure on rates on other routes.

Along with several other major carriers, Delta has also increased its passenger capacity from many European centres. Its regional European director for cargo sales Damita Waterfall said overall she was pleased with the market.
In contrast to the general increase in cargo capacity, American Airlines had decreased its freight lift by changing aircraft to Boeing 767-200 from a mix of Airbus A300, and MD11s.

Southern U.S. cities such as Miami, Orlando and Atlanta which not only attract holidaymakers but also have good trucking connections, were most vulnerable to the rate cutting, carriers and forwarding agents said.
Routine cargo continued to feature hi-technology goods like computer parts.
On ex-UK routes to Latin America, some carriers said inward investment had not reached the critical mass needed to support all scheduled flights.

Rates to Latin America reflected extra capacity from most directions. These reflected both cheap rates to Miami cutting transhipment costs and European carriers competing more aggressively ex-UK in efforts to fill flights to Latin America. - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel+ 44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 - www.racs.com
